---
title: "Plan your four weeks with ChatGPT: research first, then decide"
subtitle: "About one hour"
---

::: {.callout-tip title="In short"}
- **The idea.** Before you decide what to learn, ask ChatGPT what the field
  expects, with sources. Then add what only you know: your specialty, how you
  learn, and what worries you.
- **What you do.** Ask ChatGPT to research what doctors in training should
  know about AI, open two of its sources, let it interview you, and build
  your plan.
- **What you keep.** A plan for the four weeks, with one topic a week to
  learn with AI, and a journal template.
- **Short on time?** Read "The list you cannot finish", then do the setup and
  steps 1, 3 and 4. That is the Thursday session.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Set up ChatGPT for the course, with a project that keeps your chats
   together.
2. Asked ChatGPT to research what medical educators think doctors in training
   should know about AI, and checked two of its sources yourself.
3. Worked with ChatGPT to turn that research, and your own goals and
   background, into a plan for the four weeks, with one topic a week to learn
   with AI.
4. Saved the plan in a form you will use: a document, a spreadsheet, or
   slides, plus your journal template.
5. Decided whether to share your plan with your classmates.
6. Learned how to come back to the plan each week and change it.

Course competencies: AIM-5 (clinical use), AIM-9 (research and scholarship),
AIM-X (professional identity).
:::

**What you need.** A laptop and your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot
account. Nothing to install. Nothing in this chapter involves a patient. This
chapter is the Thursday 15 October hands-on session; if you miss the session,
do it on your own.

## The list you cannot finish

It is Thursday of week 1. You have sat through three talks. You have an
interview next Tuesday and a sub-internship evaluation you are still waiting
for. The course offers a core chapter and a menu of others each week, guest
talks in cardiology, pediatrics, and psychiatry, and a set of open labs. You have about
eight hours a week. You cannot do all of it, and nobody has told you which
parts matter for you.

You will have this problem again on the first day of every rotation in
residency. There is a reading list nobody finishes, and a senior who says
"read what matters." The residents who handle it well do two things in order.
First they find out what the field expects: the rotation's goals, what the
attendings ask about, what the specialty's own guidance says. Then they
compare that with what they already know and want, and choose.

That is research before deciding. A chatbot can do much of the first step in a
few minutes, if you ask it to show its sources. The second step is yours. This
chapter does both, and at the end you have a plan for the next four weeks that
started with evidence and fits you.

## Why this matters

This is your first real task with ChatGPT in the course, and it is not patient
care on purpose. The stakes are low, the topic is you, and you will know at
once whether the answer fits. That makes it a good way to learn what the tool
can do: search the web, summarize, interview you, and make a document or a
spreadsheet. You will use the same features later on harder problems.

The habit is the bigger point. When you bring any problem to a chatbot, a
general question gets a general answer. "What should I learn about AI?" gets
the same list for everyone. If you first ask what is already known, with
sources, and then add your own situation, the answer is about your problem.
This works for a learning plan, a quality-improvement project, or a talk you
have to give. It is the same order you use with a patient: gather the
history and the evidence before you decide.

## How it works

### Ask for research, not an answer

ChatGPT can search the web while it answers. When it does, it shows links to
the pages it used. It usually searches on its own when a question needs
current information; if an answer has no links, ask it to search.

Ask, then check. Most of the links will be real and on topic, but a link is
not proof. A chatbot can attach a real link to a claim the page does not make.
So you open two of its sources and read what they actually say. The
[foundations chapter](core-foundations.qmd) explains why this happens; here
you only need the habit.

### You decide

The research tells you what educators and professional groups think matters.
It cannot tell you that you are going into psychiatry, that you learn best by
building something, or that you are worried about what to say when a patient
asks whether AI wrote your note. Only you know that. A good plan uses both:
the field's view, so you do not miss something important, and your own, so
you actually follow it.

### One topic a week, learned with AI

The main hands-on work of the course is [Learn it with
AI](../course/learn-with-ai.qmd): 2 to 4 hours a week, on your own, using AI
to teach yourself a topic you choose. Your plan names that topic for each
week. It can be the same topic all four weeks.

### A plan that changes

The plan is a first draft. In week 2 a talk will interest you more than you
expected, or a chapter will turn out to matter less. When that happens, bring
the plan back to ChatGPT and change it. Each week's [learning
journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd) asks what you chose to learn and why,
so the plan and the journal work together.

## Set up ChatGPT

Use a laptop, not a phone: you will copy long prompts and open links side by
side. Use your university account. At CU Anschutz that is **ChatGPT Edu**; the
Canvas page "Get your ChatGPT Edu account" explains how to get it. If your
ChatGPT Edu account is not ready, use your university Microsoft Copilot
account today, and move your work over later.

1. Go to [chatgpt.com](https://chatgpt.com) and sign in with your university
   email.
2. Check the bottom left of the screen. At CU Anschutz it should say
   **"CU - Anschutz (Edu)"**. If it does not, you are in a personal account.
   Say so in the session, or ask at office hours.
3. Make a **project** for this course. Find **Projects** in the left sidebar,
   make a new one, and name it "AI in Medicine". A project keeps the chats for
   this course together, so you can come back to them.
4. Start a new chat inside the project.

No Projects in your account? Start a chat named AI in Medicine.

## Do: build your plan

**In the session** (about 40 minutes): set up, then steps 1, 3 and 4. Step 2
is optional. **After the session, before tonight's journal** (about 10
minutes): steps 5 and 6. Step 7 is for the weeks ahead.

Copy each prompt into the same chat, in order. Fill in the parts in brackets
first. ChatGPT remembers what came earlier in the chat, so each step builds on
the last.

### 1. Prepare: gather what the field says (in the session, 10 minutes)

```
I'm a fourth-year medical student applying in
[your specialty, or "undecided"]. I'm starting a
four-week course on AI in medicine.

Search the web for what medical educators and
professional groups say doctors in training should
know about AI. Look for curriculum frameworks,
competency lists, and statements from groups such as
the AAMC or specialty societies, from the last three
years. Also look for what AI is changing in
[your specialty].

List 6 to 10 sources. For each one, give who wrote it,
the year, the link, and one sentence on what it says.
```

Now **open two of the links.** Does the page exist? Does it say what ChatGPT
said it says? Write down what you found. That is your check for question 2 of
this week's [learning journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd).

### 2. Summarize: find the themes (optional, 5 minutes)

If you have time, ask for the themes. If not, go straight to step 3.

```
Group what these sources say into 4 to 6 themes: the
things doctors in training are expected to know or be
able to do about AI. For each theme, name the sources
that support it. Mark any theme that only one source
supports.
```

### 3. Decide: let it interview you (in the session, 10 minutes)

```
Now interview me, one question at a time, about what I
want from this course: my background, what I have
tried with AI so far, what worries me about it, how I
learn best, and where AI might help my work as a
resident.

After about six questions, suggest 3 to 5 learning
goals in my own words. Link each goal to a source or
theme from the research, or say that it is mine alone.
Then ask me what I want to change.
```

Answer each question in a sentence or two. There are no wrong answers. If you
do not know what you want yet, say that; it is a useful answer.

When ChatGPT suggests your goals, **make them yours.** Change anything that
does not sound like you. Ask for a goal to be smaller, bigger, or more about
your specialty. Keep going until you would be happy to show the goals to a
colleague. A goal that is yours alone, with no source behind it, is fine.

### 4. Create: make your plan (in the session, 10 minutes)

ChatGPT cannot read this book's website, so the prompt below includes what
the course offers. Copy all of it.

```
Turn my goals into a plan for the four weeks, using
what my course offers (below). For each week, list
the talks, chapters, or labs I will use, one topic I
will learn with AI (2 to 4 hours, on my own), and how
I will know it worked. Keep it to about 8 to 10 hours
a week, including sessions. Leave room to change it.
Then tell me which of my goals the course does not
cover, so I can learn them with AI.

What my course offers:
Week 1: How these systems work (how AI models learn,
  and why chatbots make things up). Thursday: this
  planning session.
Week 2: Prompting lab (getting good answers, and
  knowing their limits). Also: Critical appraisal
  (checking AI tools, their answers, and the evidence);
  Bias and equity; Grounding AI in real sources
  (tools that answer from documents you give them).
Week 3: Talking to patients about AI. Also: Agentic
  coding (build a small clinical tool, then test it);
  an ambient scribe lab (draft a note from a recorded
  visit, then check it).
Week 4: Ethics: what you owe when you sign a note
  drafted by AI. Also: Will AI take your job?; What AI
  costs the planet.
Every week: talks, guest talks from clinicians in
  several specialties, and a weekly learning journal.
Every week, on my own: Learn it with AI, 2 to 4 hours
  using AI to teach myself a topic I choose. This is
  the main hands-on work of the course.
```

The [syllabus](../course/syllabus.qmd) has the same list with links to each
chapter.

Ask for the plan in the form you will use: a table, a Word document, a
spreadsheet, or a few slides. ChatGPT can make a file you download. If that
does not work, copy the table into Word or Google Docs. Save it in a document
you will keep, named "AI in Medicine plan". Your chat stays in the project, so
you can come back to it.

### 5. Create: your journal template (after the session, 5 minutes)

Before tonight's journal, make your journal template in the same chat:

```
Using my goals, make a weekly learning journal
template I can fill in within 30 minutes, as a short
markdown template.

It must include these five course questions:
1. What I chose to learn, and why
2. How AI helped, and where it got in the way
   (including one time I felt I needed to check
   the AI: how I checked, and what I found)
3. What surprised me
4. What changed for me
5. What I used, and whether it was worth my time

Add one or two headings of your own that connect each
entry to my goals.
```

Move, rename, or cut the extra headings until the template suits how you
think. The five course questions stay. Add the template to your "AI in
Medicine plan" document.

### 6. Share, if you want to (after the session, 5 minutes)

Sharing is optional, and it helps. Hearing what classmates want from the
course is often the most useful part of the week, and it is how a group of
students becomes a learning community. Some ways, from least to most:

- Type one of your goals in the Zoom chat, if the session has time left.
- Bring one goal to your Friday small group.
- If you have joined the course Discord, post your plan, or one goal, in
  **#show-and-tell**.
- Put your plan in this week's learning journal, so you can look back at it in
  week 4.

Share only what you are comfortable sharing. If you keep the plan private,
that is fine.

### 7. Follow through: come back each week

The plan is meant to change. Each week:

1. Open the "AI in Medicine" project and start a new chat.
2. Paste in your plan and your last journal entry.
3. Ask:

```
Here is my learning plan and my last journal entry.
What did I do, what did I skip, and what should I
change for next week? Ask me before you change
anything.
```

Start a new chat each week rather than one long one. Very long chats can lose
track of what was said earlier. Your document carries what matters from week
to week.

## Check

Look at your plan and ask:

| Check | A good plan |
|---|---|
| The research is in it | You can say which theme or source led to each part, or that the part is yours alone |
| You are in it | It mentions your specialty, how you learn, or what worries you, not only the course's topics |
| You checked something | You opened two sources and know whether they said what ChatGPT said |
| You learn with AI each week | Each week names one topic you will learn with AI, and why you chose it |
| It fits | About 8 to 10 hours a week, with room to change |
| It can change | You know when you will look at it again, and how |

: What a good plan looks like. {#tbl-check}

## Standing question

Go back to Thursday morning and the list you could not finish. You still
cannot do all of it. But you now know what the field thinks matters, which
of those things the course covers, and which ones you care about.

Two of this week's [journal](../course/learning-journal.qmd) questions fit
this session. For question 1, what you chose to learn and why, name one goal
you kept that no source told you to. For question 3, what surprised you, say
what the research showed you that you would not have picked on your own.

## The rules

The course has four rules:

> Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account. Never put real patient
> information into a course activity. Check what matters before you rely on
> it. You sign the note.

What counts as patient information is on [its own
page](../course/patient-information.qmd).

## Go deeper

- OpenAI, [Plan something from start to
  finish](https://learn.chatgpt.com/training/hands-on/work) (about 20 to 25
  minutes): a guided practice that runs in your browser with sample data, so
  you do not need an account. You plan a team dinner in the same six steps
  this chapter uses: prepare, summarize, decide, create, share, follow
  through. It uses ChatGPT Work, which your account may not have; this
  chapter's Do works in an ordinary chat.
- OpenAI, [ChatGPT Training](https://learn.chatgpt.com/training): short
  walkthroughs on projects, documents and slides, and voice. Several use
  ChatGPT Work, which your account may not have.
- OpenAI, [Projects and chats](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/projects): when
  to use a project, and what it keeps.
- [What the field expects](../appendix/competency-frameworks.qmd): the AAMC's
  work and the published AI competency frameworks for medical students. Use it
  to check what your research in step 1 found, and what it missed.
